cues.text: Three Shepherd Children of Aljustrel

In the village of Aljustrel , near Fátima, Portugal, three cousins tended sheep together: ten-year-old Lúcia dos Santos and her younger cousins, nine-year-old Francisco Marto and seven-year-old Jacinta Marto .
Portugal in 1917 was gripped by a fiercely anti-clerical republic and, beyond its borders, by the slaughter of the First World War.
Into this uncertainty, the children lived an unremarkable rural life of prayer, play, and pasture.
God, as He so often does, chose the smallest and least equipped to carry His largest message.
An Angel's Preparation

The year before the apparitions of Our Lady began, the three children reported being visited three times by a figure identifying himself as the Angel of Peace , who taught them to pray and to offer up sacrifices for sinners.
This quiet preparation mattered: when the Lady herself finally appeared, the children were already accustomed to a discipline of prayer far beyond their years.
We see here a pattern true of every soul Heaven prepares for a mission: grace builds gradually, in hidden faithfulness, long before the decisive moment arrives.
A Lady Brighter Than the Sun
On May 13, 1917 , the children were at play near a small holm oak at a place called the Cova da Iria .
There they saw a flash of light and then a woman "brighter than the sun," dressed in white and gold, holding a rosary.
She asked them to return to that same spot on the thirteenth of each month for five months, and to pray the Rosary daily for peace and for the end of the war.
She did not ask for grand penances or public recognition.
She asked, simply, for prayer, offered faithfully.
Secrets Entrusted to Children
At the third apparition, on July 13, 1917 , the Lady entrusted the children with what became known as the three secrets of Fátima.
They included a vision of souls in torment and a call to consecrate Russia to her Immaculate Heart to avert further war.
She told them, too, that Francisco and Jacinta would soon be called to Heaven, while Lúcia would remain to spread devotion to her Immaculate Heart.
Even very young children, the events of Fátima insist, can be entrusted with a weight of responsibility that would stagger an adult, so long as they remain, as these three did, humble and obedient.
Arrest and a Delayed Apparition
Alarmed by the growing crowds, the local civil administrator seized the children on August 13 and held them under threat of execution by boiling oil, trying to force them to recant.
They would not.
Denied their monthly appointment at the Cova, they instead received the Lady's apparition privately on August 19 , once released.
Their quiet steadfastness under real threat, at ages seven to ten, remains one of the most striking details of the entire episode: they simply would not say what was not true.
The Miracle of the Sun
By the final apparition on October 13, 1917 , word had spread across Portugal, and an estimated seventy thousand people, believers and skeptics alike, crowded into the rain-soaked Cova da Iria.

As the Lady identified herself as "Our Lady of the Rosary" and departed, witnesses across the crowd reported the sun appearing to spin, throw off colored light, and plunge toward the earth before returning to its place.
Even the secular press of Lisbon reported the event the next day.
Francisco died of influenza in 1919 at age ten; Jacinta followed in 1920 at age nine, offering her sufferings, as the Lady had asked, for the conversion of sinners.
Legacy
The local bishop, José Alves Correia da Silva , declared the apparitions "worthy of belief" on October 13, 1930 , after thirteen years of careful investigation.

Lúcia lived on as a Carmelite nun until 2005, and both Francisco and Jacinta were canonized by Pope Francis in 2017, on the apparitions' hundredth anniversary; Lúcia herself was declared Venerable in 2023.

Fátima still speaks to a world no less anxious than that of 1917: that the smallest, most childlike acts of daily prayer and sacrifice are never wasted, and that Our Lady's Immaculate Heart remains, as she promised, our refuge.
